title: Continuous Discovery in One Page
intro: The team that builds the product talks to customers every week, together, aimed at one outcome.

learn.title: What makes it continuous
learn.text:
Project research happens before a big decision and then stops.

**Continuous discovery:** the team building the product has a customer touchpoint **at least every week**, in small activities aimed at one outcome.

Every decision keeps meeting fresh evidence.

try.q: What is the minimum cadence of customer contact?
try.explain: Weekly is the floor, not the target.

learn.title: The product trio
learn.text:
A **product manager, a designer and an engineer** interview together.

When all three hear the same stories, they argue less about whose information is right and more about what to do.

try.q: Why should the trio interview together?
options: They build a shared view from the same stories
It cuts the number of interviews needed
Engineers can answer the technical questions live during the call
Customers trust a bigger group more
try.explain: Shared evidence reduces arguments based on different information.

learn.title: The loop
learn.text:
**Outcome** → **opportunities** heard in stories → about three **solutions** for one target → **assumption tests**.

Test results send you back to the opportunity map, not straight to the backlog.

try.explain: The loop closes on the map, which keeps the next choice informed.

learn.title: Habits to start with
learn.text:
**Automate recruiting**, so next week’s interview is already booked.
**Write a one-page snapshot** after each interview and share it.
**Refresh the map** every three to four interviews.
**Story-map an idea** to list its assumptions: 20 to 30 minutes.

try.q: What keeps weekly interviews from stalling?
options: Recruiting that runs on its own
A dedicated research team that books everything
try.explain: If recruiting is manual, the habit dies the first busy week.

learn.title: Where to start
learn.text:
**Feature factory:** story-map one planned feature and list its hidden assumptions.
**Messy middle:** make one bright spot: the trio interviews together.
**Sliding back under pressure:** share snapshots and the map after every interview.

try.q: Stakeholders under pressure are asking for specific features again. First step?
options: Share a snapshot after every interview
Pause discovery until things calm down
Run a large survey to settle it
try.explain: Showing your work rebuilds trust in the evidence.

options: Small research activities every week, aimed at one outcome
A research phase before each new project
A quarterly study run by a research team
Customer feedback collected and reviewed after each major release
test.explain: It runs alongside delivery, not before it.

test.q: Who is in the product trio?
test.explain: The people who decide and build the product.

test.q: What is the order of the discovery loop?
test.explain: Start from the outcome; solutions come only after a target opportunity.

test.q: How often should the opportunity map be refreshed?
options: Once a quarter, together with roadmap planning
test.explain: Often enough to stay current without chasing every story.

test.q: A team works from a fixed roadmap and counts features shipped. Best first step?
options: Story-map one feature and list its assumptions
Rewrite the whole roadmap as outcomes
Hire a dedicated researcher before changing anything else
test.explain: It needs no permission and shows the risk in the plan.

test.q: How long does story-mapping an idea’s assumptions take?
options: Two or three full working days
test.explain: Short enough to do for every idea.
